I am buying a 2000 cannon combination safe. Not one of the shitty new digital ones. Can anyone tell me legit if quality was better in 2000 or if it has gotten worse?
Old gun safes vs new gun safes

Why exactly are the digital ones shitty?

Quality is often more dependent on brand. I buy Liberty for a reason.
The digital lock will break much sooner than the combination lock. The mechanical combo lock will last out your grand children and never need any batteries.

Don't know about that specific model, but if you go to any sports goods store and flick or tap the sides of these new safes, the hollow noise of thin metal will tell you all you need to know. A good safe should feel like you're flicking a brick wall.

The question is, how thick and sturdy is everything other the front door? On the crappy ones, the front is thick and sturdy and you can cut through the sides and the back with a can opener. There are some really good new ones but most are not. Many are merely big filing cabinets with fancy fronts. Check out youtube. There are lots of videos of people breaking into gun safes with a simple pry bar.
Go check if there is a "how to" on breaking in. Most safes can delay theft but not prevent it.

How about a guide to figure out if the safe you want is good for you, with some info on past safes.

First, and foremost, the absolute most important security feature of a safe, is that no one knows you have the safe. Break that, and no safe within any reasonable budget is going to stop a determined thief. So don't go wasting your money on the whole showboat, heirloom nonsense. It is hard to conceal large gun safes, but find a way if possible.

Now the nitty-gritty: Get a model number off that used safe and get specs. You wont be able to just judge by the year.

  1. Gauge (thickness of metal) For BOTH the door and the walls. 12 = shit, 10 = good-ish, 8 &below= king
  2. Locking Mechanism. Preference and use dependent. Default? Mechanical is better. All Metal
  3. Bolts (placement, number.) 4 sided is best, the more/the thicker-the better.
  4. Fire Rating (Underwriters Laboratory Inc Certified or don’t bother) Search the Letter ratings.
  5. Weight. A safe that claims to have the thick gauge will not be light. If it’s 6ft, and less then 1000 lbs, it’s a cabinet-not a safe.

These guys make the best bang for your buck, secure safes. IMO https://www.sturdysafe.com/

New safes are mostly a flimsy 12 gauge siding with a 10 gauge door, with the sidings 'reinforced' by the insulation, giving them the salable-appearance of being much thicker. The more expensive, name-brand safes offer to step the sides up to 10 gauge for a considerable amount of extra money. There is 18 years of inflation between the safe you are looking at and the new ones. You bet your ass there has been cost cutting, and my bet is it is in the Gauge. I'd be willing to bet that year 2000 safe has a higher chance of being 10 gauge, but that is by no means a guarantee

Locking Mechanism. If this is a safe you want to open multiple times a day, every day, digital is a fine choice, but don’t fuck yourself and get one without a mechanical backup. If this is a once a day or every so often opener. Just get the mechanical. With proper maintenance, as well as it not being some of the new locks that use plastic parts, it can last a long time. Each one has draw backs depending on the thief. Someone might have a simple hack to get past a digital, and someone else might have the experience to defeat that one mechanical lock. What are the chances a pro of either persuasion is going to be at your safe in the first place?

Bolts are simple. You want them on all 4 sides as a basic pry prevention. Some have just the 3 sided and internal hinges on the 1 non bolt side; Which is meh, but not a deal breaker. The amount scales to size and you just have to judge yourself.

Fire rating. If it is important to you that you're valuables be protected from fire. Do not get a safe that is not certified by Underwriter Labs (UL.) There is a bunch of backstory and history I can’t recall nor am interested in adding to this already huge post. UL or bust, fuck anyone who says otherwise.

Weight. It’s explained well in the bullet point, but to expand; Thick metal weights more. A terrible, 11 gauge, Liberty Brand, 6x3x3ish safe is 980lbs. I would guess an 8 gauge equivalent would be nearly twice that, at the least 1500lbs. It’s a fast way to spot a fake, or pick out shitty safes with no detailed specs.
